p.x:
My name is Somchai, and I live in Bangkok, a very big city. My flat is in a tall building near the river. From my window, I can see a bridge and lots of boats.
The city is exciting, but it's also very noisy. There is a lot of traffic, especially in the morning, so I go to work by motorbike. The air is often polluted too. My office is in the city centre. The pavements are often busy with food stalls, so walking can be difficult.
At the weekend, I like to go to Lumpini Park. It's quiet there, and people run, cycle and do exercise. You can even see big lizards near the lake! Bangkok is quite safe, but at night I am careful in some streets. My parents live in a small village, and they think Bangkok is too dangerous. But I love it here.

Five years ago, Anna sold her car. "I spent two hours a day in traffic during rush hour," she explains. "It was crazy." Now she uses public transport, rides a bicycle, or walks. She says her life has improved in many ways.
First, it's cheaper. She doesn't pay for petrol, parking or repairs. Second, she is fitter, because she walks or cycles at least forty minutes a day. And third, she knows her district much better. "When you drive, you only see the road. As a pedestrian, you notice the local shops and cafés, and you meet your neighbours."
Of course, there are problems. Some areas still have poor facilities for cyclists, and crossing a busy road can be frightening when every vehicle is in a hurry. On hot days, she arrives at work covered in sweat. She also worries about bike theft, which is the most common crime in her area.
Nevertheless, Anna thinks more cities should be designed for people, not cars. "Look at the skyscrapers downtown," she says. "We build amazing towers, but we still haven't made it easy to walk to them. Good urban planning should make car-free life convenient for everyone."

Today, more than half of the world's population lives in cities, and by 2050 the figure is expected to reach nearly 70%. Some metropolises, such as Tokyo or Jakarta, have more inhabitants than many countries. This rapid growth has created vibrant, cosmopolitan centres where people from all over the world live and work side by side.
But growth brings challenges. As cities expand outwards, urban sprawl swallows farmland and forces residents into long journeys. Where land is scarce, developers build upwards instead, and high-rise towers replace historic neighbourhoods. Even famous landmarks can find themselves surrounded by glass and concrete.
Gentrification adds another layer of complexity. When a poor area becomes fashionable, new cafés and galleries arrive, amenities improve, and property values rise. For newcomers, the area becomes more attractive; for long-term residents, it may become unaffordable. Critics argue that cities risk becoming playgrounds for the wealthy while the number of homeless people grows. Overcrowded flats on the edge of town are often the only option for low-paid workers who keep the city running. The challenge for planners is to allow cities to grow without pushing out the very people who made them interesting in the first place.

q.th: ผู้อยู่อาศัยเดิมอาจจ่ายไม่ไหว
x: For newcomers it becomes more attractive.
สำหรับคนใหม่ พื้นที่น่าสนใจขึ้น
Cities may become playgrounds for the wealthy.
เมืองอาจกลายเป็นสนามเด็กเล่นของคนรวย
New cafés arrive and do well.
ร้านกาแฟใหม่เข้ามา

q.s: What is the writer's main concern in the last paragraph?
o: Cities should grow without pushing out the people who made them interesting.
Homeless people should leave the city.
q.en: '…allow cities to grow without pushing out the very people who made them interesting.'
q.th: ให้เมืองเติบโตโดยไม่ผลักไสคนที่ทำให้เมืองน่าสนใจ
x: The writer wants them to grow.
ผู้เขียนอยากให้เมืองเติบโต
The writer is concerned about them.
ผู้เขียนเป็นห่วงพวกเขา
